/superpowers-ross:brainstorming

I want to build our dedicated image upload mechanism, which should be a dialog launched from different places, currently the profile page. It should accept the image as drag and drop as well as finding a file. A single file only. The image should then be resized in the browser before upload, using a mechanism which maintains good image quality, not just a naive resize which will leave it looking jagged. Then the upload to the API runs, and we get back the pending image, which we should poll every few seconds to see what the result is, or perhaps a gradual backoff on the polling. Only when the image is accepted do we show the result. What else do we need to consider?
I'll start by reading how images work today on both sides: the frontend image doc, the API's image endpoints in `openapi.json`, the roadmap lines, and the profile page.
Read the image-handling doc, roadmap, and the API's upload/poll endpoint contracts; checked the existing PhotoField and profile write actions, and how a photo attaches to a profile.

I read the upload and poll endpoints in `openapi.json`, `docs/image-handling.md`, `../api/docs/bunny.md`, the roadmap lines and the current `PhotoField`. The API has already settled several things you listed as open, and a few of them differ from what you described.

## What the API contract already decides

- **The polling schedule is set by the API, and it is faster than every few seconds.** The description on `POST /api/member/images` says to poll first at 400 ms and then every 500 ms, and to stop at 10 seconds. A night image usually settles in about a quarter of a second and a day image in under one. After 10 seconds nothing more can be learned for at least five minutes, because the first classifier attempt has failed and the retry waits. A backoff would only delay a result that normally arrives in under a second, so I recommend following the contract.
- **An image still checking after 10 seconds needs its own copy.** The contract says to tell the member it is taking longer than usual and to check again the next time they open the page. The image cannot be attached before it is `READY`, so something has to remember its id in the meantime.
- **The result can be `READY`, `REFUSED` (with a classification) or `CHECK_FAILED`.** `CHECK_FAILED` means nobody judged the image, and the copy should invite a fresh upload rather than read as a refusal. Roadmap line 465 plans to stop sending the classification to the uploader, so the refusal copy should not depend on it.
- **The side is fixed when the image is uploaded.** `side` is a required query parameter. A night-classified image uploaded on day is refused, and the profile write answers `409 IMAGE_SIDE_MISMATCH` for an image from the other side. The dialog therefore takes `side` as a prop.
- **The upload errors each need copy:** `400 IMAGE_UNREADABLE` (not JPEG, PNG or WebP, or over 50 megapixels), `400 UPLOAD_UNREADABLE`, `413 IMAGE_TOO_LARGE` (over 10 MB), `429 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` (30 uploads in 24 hours), `403 ACCOUNT_RESTRICTED`, and `503 IMAGE_BUSY`, which spends nothing and can be retried automatically.
- **The server reduces every image to 1280 px on the long edge.** The browser should therefore resize to 1280 as well. `docs/image-handling.md` says member photos are 1400 on the long edge, which contradicts the API, and the doc needs correcting as part of this work.

## Resizing in the browser

- **Canvas quality differs by browser.** `imageSmoothingQuality: 'high'` gives a good result in Chrome, while Firefox and Safari give a noticeably softer or more aliased one on a large reduction. The two reliable options are halving step by step on the canvas, or the `pica` library, which uses a Lanczos filter. `pica` runs in a Web Worker and can use WebAssembly, so it would need `worker-src blob:` and possibly `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` added to `lib/security/csp.ts`. Both are the deliberate CSP decisions `CLAUDE.md` asks for. I will set out the options properly when we reach approaches.
- **Decoding in the browser means we accept whatever the browser can open.** Safari on a Mac decodes HEIC, so an iPhone photograph uploads as a JPEG even though the API refuses HEIC. Chrome cannot decode HEIC, so that case needs its own error copy.
- **EXIF orientation has to be applied before drawing** (`createImageBitmap(file, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })`), or phone portraits upload sideways. Drawing to a canvas also removes the location data before the file leaves the device.
- **Smaller cases:** an image already under 1280 px should not be enlarged. PNG transparency needs a white background before encoding to JPEG. An animated GIF becomes its first frame. Safari's `toBlob` cannot encode WebP, so JPEG at about 0.92 is the portable output, and the server re-encodes it once more. iOS Safari limits canvas area to about 16.7 megapixels, which rules out drawing a large photograph onto a full-size intermediate canvas.

## Integration with this codebase

- **The upload needs a route to the API.** The generated client is server-only. A server action refuses a body over 1 MB by default (`serverActions.bodySizeLimit`), so an upload through a server action needs that limit raised. The other route is a browser `fetch` to `/api/member/images` through the existing rewrite, which breaks the rule that client components do not call the API directly. Server actions from one page also run one at a time, so a poll every 500 ms would hold up any other action on the page.
- **Attaching the image is a separate step.** A profile photo attaches through `imageId` on `PUT /api/member/me/day-profile` or `night-profile`. Those endpoints replace the whole profile, and `lib/profile/actions.ts` already copies the current `imageId` forward.
- **Leftover images should be deleted.** If the member closes the dialog while an image is checking, or uploads a second one, the first stays unattached. `DELETE /api/member/images/{id}` removes it, and each abandoned upload counts towards the 30-per-day allowance.
- **Drag and drop needs a keyboard route and a touch route.** The drop area must work as a button, and a phone offers no drag at all. A drop of several files, or of something other than an image, needs a message.
- **Tests cannot exercise the resize.** happy-dom has no canvas, so the resize has to sit behind a small interface that tests replace with a stub, and resize quality has to be checked by eye in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
- **Out of scope unless you want them:** a crop control (listed as not built in `image-handling.md`), removing a photo, and pasting an image from the clipboard.

## First question

The profile page is one form with a single Save button. The photo lives in the read-only header panel, and today `PhotoField` only shows a local preview.

When the image comes back `READY`, what should happen?

1. **Attach it straight away (my recommendation).** The dialog's confirm button saves the photo to the profile on its own, and the header updates. This works the same way on every future caller: a diary entry or a mail can take the `READY` image, while the profile attaches immediately. The existing actions read the current profile from the API rather than from the form, so unsaved text edits elsewhere on the page are neither lost nor saved by accident.
2. **Stage it into the form.** The dialog hands back the image id, the header shows the new photo as pending, and nothing is saved until the member presses Save. This matches the one-button model, but an image left unsaved stays in storage until the reaper removes it.
Attach it straight away, this is separate to the rest of the form. Does the API allow that save without also saving what's currently in the form?
Checked whether a profile write clears fields it omits, and how the night write detaches the old image.

Yes. The API has no partial update, but the photo can still be saved without anything from the form.

## What the API does

`PUT /api/member/me/day-profile` and `night-profile` replace the whole profile. I checked `DayProfileService.update`, `NightProfileService.update` and `ProfileUpdate.apply` in `../api`:

- The service builds the new profile from the request alone, so a field left out of the request is cleared.
- If `imageId` is left out, the current photo is detached and its stored files are deleted once the transaction commits.
- If `imageId` names a different image, the new image is attached and the old one is detached and deleted. Replacing a photo therefore removes the old one, and nothing needs to clean it up afterwards.
- Both services lock the member row first, so two writes at the same moment cannot leave an image attached with no profile pointing at it.

## How the photo action works

The photo action is a server action. It reads the profile with `getOwnDayProfile` or `getOwnNightProfile`, then writes back exactly what the API returned, changing only `imageId`. The unsaved values in the form never reach it, because it reads nothing from the form. `saveProfile` and `saveNightProfile` already work this way in the other direction: they read the current `image.id` from the API and send it back unchanged. The form and the photo action each preserve the other's part.

Two consequences of that design:

- **The two writes could clash in one case.** If a form save read the profile, the photo was then attached, and the form save wrote afterwards, the form save would send the old image id. That old image would already be deleted, so the save would fail rather than quietly put the old photo back. One tab cannot produce that order, because the dialog is modal and Next runs a page's server actions one at a time. Two tabs could produce it, and the member would see a failed save. I think that is acceptable without an API change.
- **Stored text is screened again on every write.** Sending the current description back runs it through the contact-details and link screen once more. That screen normally passes text it already passed. If its rules have tightened since the text was saved, the photo write would answer `422 TEXT_NOT_ALLOWED` for a field the member never touched, so that error needs its own copy.

A dedicated `PUT /api/member/me/day-profile/image` would avoid both problems and would also give a clean way to remove a photo. It would be an (API) roadmap line. I recommend building without it now and adding it only if removing a photo comes into scope.

## Next question

You said the result is shown only once the image is accepted. I want to check where that applies.

While the image is being checked, which usually takes under a second but can take up to 10 seconds, what should the dialog show?

1. **The member's own resized photograph with a "Checking" state (my recommendation).** The profile header does not change until the image is `READY` and attached. The image is already on the member's own device, so showing it to them exposes nothing, and they can see they picked the right file. The API's suggestion of its blurred 32-pixel placeholder adds nothing next to the real photograph.
2. **Only a progress state, with no image**, until the image is `READY`. The dialog then shows the checked image as the API serves it.

Let's add a PUT for the profile image to both sides in the API as part of this work. 
Let's show the blurred image back from the server if we have that while it is being checked

Agreed on both.

The blurred image is always available once the upload has been accepted. `POST /api/member/images` returns an `ImageView`, and `placeholderDataUrl` is a required field on it, so the dialog can show it as soon as the upload answers. Before that answer the dialog has no server image yet, because it is still resizing and uploading. That stage shows a progress state with no image. The placeholder is 32 pixels wide, so it will be scaled up to fill the preview space, which is why it looks blurred.

For the API work, the endpoints would be `PUT /api/member/me/day-profile/image` and `PUT /api/member/me/night-profile/image`, each taking `{ imageId }`. Each one reuses `ProfileUpdate.apply`, so it keeps the row lock, the side-mismatch conflict, and the deletion of the replaced image. It also completes the profile-photo checklist award, as the full write does today. The night endpoint keeps the same gates as the full night write, which are verification and an open night side. The text screen does not run, because no text is sent. The full profile `PUT` requests still carry `imageId` after this change, so the form actions keep sending it back unchanged. The alternative would be to drop `imageId` from those requests and make the image endpoint the only way to change the photo. I recommend dropping it: two ways to write the same field is how the two-tab clash above happens, and without it the form save can never touch the photo. That is an API contract change, so both form actions change in the same piece of work.

## Next question

Once there is a dedicated image endpoint, removing a photo costs one more handler: `DELETE /api/member/me/day-profile/image` and the night equivalent. That handler detaches the image and deletes its files. Should removing a photo be part of this work?

1. **Yes, include removal (my recommendation).** The header gets a "Remove photo" control next to "Change photo", with a confirmation step. Today a member who uploads the wrong photograph can only replace it, and on the night side that is a real privacy gap.
2. **No, only add and replace for now.** Removal gets its own roadmap line.

Drop the imageid from the existing profile updates and remove the then dead code.
Yes also include the removal

Both noted. The full profile writes lose `imageId`, and whatever becomes dead code with it is deleted: `ProfileUpdate.apply`'s role in the full writes, the `imageId: current.image?.id` lines in `lib/profile/actions.ts` and `night-actions.ts`, and the tests that assert that value is carried forward. The image endpoints on each side become `PUT` and `DELETE` on `/api/member/me/{day,night}-profile/image`, and the header gets "Remove photo" with a confirmation step.

## Next question

What happens when an image is still `CHECKING` after 10 seconds? The API contract says it then cannot resolve for at least five minutes. It will either be retried then or reach `CHECK_FAILED` within the hour. This happens only when a classifier vendor fails to answer, so it should be rare.

1. **Stop and ask the member to try again later (my recommendation).** The dialog says the photo could not be checked right now and asks them to try again in a few minutes. It deletes the unattached image, and the profile stays as it was. Nothing needs remembering across page loads. The cost is that the upload still counts towards the 30-per-day allowance, and in the rare case the retry would have passed, the member uploads again.
2. **Remember it and attach it later.** The dialog stores the pending image id in the browser's local storage, keyed by side. The next time the profile page loads, it polls that id and attaches the image if it is `READY`. This follows the contract's "re-check when they next open the page", but it works only on the same device and browser. It also puts a pending-image state, and its copy, in the profile header.
3. **The API attaches it when the check finishes.** The new `PUT` accepts a `CHECKING` image as the pending profile photo and attaches it on publication. This works on any device, but a refusal would then need to reach the member some other way. Roadmap line 378 shows that the refusal notification is blocked on the appeal route, so this option pulls in unfinished work.
Stop and ask them to try again later, but are we sure 10 seconds is enough? Maybe the allowance should be 15 or 30 seconds
I'll check the API's timeouts before answering rather than rely on the contract's description.
Checked the API's actual check-pipeline timeouts and retry schedule, rather than trust the contract's own description of them.

No. The API's own timeouts show that 10 seconds can cut off a check that is going to pass. The contract's claim that 10 seconds is "past the classifier's own timeout" counts only the classifier, not the steps before and after it.

## What the check actually does

`ImageCheckPipeline.check` runs three steps in order on one of 8 check threads (`app.images.check.threads`), and `application.yml` bounds each one:

1. **Hash matching with Arachnid Shield**, which can take up to 8 seconds (`app.arachnid.timeout`).
2. **Classification with Rekognition**, which can take up to 8 seconds (`call-timeout: 8000ms`, split into two attempts of 3 seconds each).
3. **Publication.** A day image is copied between Bunny storage zones, and each Bunny request allows a 5-second connection and a 20-second read.

If both vendors are slow but do answer, the first two steps alone take nearly 16 seconds, and the image then passes. The API tells us to stop polling at 10 seconds, so the member would be told to try again even though the photo was about to be accepted. A queue can also form ahead of the image: each upload's check occupies a thread for as long as its vendor calls take, and the queue holds 50. When a first attempt does fail, the image stays `PENDING`. `ImageCheckRetryService` runs every 5 minutes and retries only images more than 5 minutes old, so the retry lands between 5 and 10 minutes after the upload. Polling for longer than about 30 seconds therefore gains nothing.

## Recommendation: 30 seconds, with your backoff after the first few

- Poll at 400 ms, then every 500 ms until 5 seconds have passed. Normal images settle in that window.
- After 5 seconds, poll every 2 seconds until 30 seconds have passed. A slow check is waiting on a vendor, so polling faster would not make it arrive sooner. Backing off also cuts the number of requests from about 60 to about 22.
- The dialog keeps showing the blurred image with "Checking" for the whole 30 seconds, with no separate message partway through.
- At 30 seconds the dialog stops polling, deletes the image and asks the member to try again in a few minutes.

30 seconds covers both vendors being slow plus a slow copy. It does not cover Bunny taking its full 20-second read on top of that. I think that case is rare enough to accept, since it means both vendors and the storage provider are all degraded at once. The API description on `POST /api/member/images` needs correcting to match these figures in the same change. Otherwise the next client built against it inherits the 10-second limit.

Should the dialog wait 30 seconds before giving up, or do you want a different limit?
Yes that 30 seconds with backoff as suggested, we should update the API to stop suggesting 10 seconds too
Checked the pica package and Next's server-action body-size limits.

Agreed. Both changes to `POST /api/member/images` go in: the description gets the new figures, and the 30-second limit is explained by the three steps it has to cover.

The requirements are settled, so here are the two technical choices the design depends on: how the image is resized, and how requests reach the API.

## Resizing

**A. `pica` in a Web Worker, with no WebAssembly (recommended).** `pica` (MIT, version 10.0.3, updated August 2026) resizes with a Lanczos filter. It is the same family of filter used by image editors, and it keeps edges sharp without the stair-stepping you described. It works on the source in tiles, so a 50-megapixel photograph never needs a canvas larger than iOS Safari's 16.7-megapixel limit. The worker keeps the dialog responsive while a large phone photograph is processed. The worker is built from a `blob:` URL, so the CSP needs `worker-src 'self' blob:`. That is a widening, but it names no third-party origin. I would leave WebAssembly off, which avoids adding `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` as well. The JavaScript filter handles one image to 1280 pixels in a few hundred milliseconds, so WebAssembly would not change what the member experiences.

**B. Our own step-down on a canvas, with no dependency.** This halves the image repeatedly with `imageSmoothingQuality: 'high'` until the next halving would drop below 1280, then does one final draw. Each halving averages four pixels into one, so the result is far better than a single large reduction. It is still visibly softer than Lanczos on fine detail such as hair and text. The work also runs on the main thread, and a large source needs intermediate canvases that exceed the iOS area limit, so it would have to be decoded at a smaller size first.

**C. `createImageBitmap` with `resizeQuality: 'high'`.** This is the least code of the three. Its quality depends on each browser's implementation, and I do not know for certain that Safari honours the resize options, so I would not rely on it.

In all three, decoding goes through `createImageBitmap(file, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' })`, and the output is a JPEG at 0.92 on a white background. The server re-encodes it to WebP at 0.90.

## Reaching the API

**A. Server actions for everything (recommended).** Upload, poll, attach, remove and delete all use server actions, which follows the rule that the generated client is server-only. A resized 1280-pixel JPEG is usually 300 KB to 1 MB, which can go over the default 1 MB server action body limit. `serverActions.bodySizeLimit` rises to `'3mb'` in `next.config.ts`. The costs are that no upload progress percentage is available, so the dialog shows "Uploading" without a figure, and that polls queue behind any other action on the page. While the dialog is open nothing else on the page can run an action, so that queue is always empty.

**B. A browser request to `/api/member/images` through the existing rewrite.** This would give an upload progress bar through `XMLHttpRequest`. It breaks the server-only rule for one call and duplicates the error handling that `lib/api` already provides. At the file sizes above, the progress bar is visible only on a slow mobile connection.

Do you agree with `pica` in a worker and server actions throughout? If so, I will present the design section by section.

A. Pica
I don't think we should have that rule that everything is a server action, it was probably written just to give the impression of a retro website, but I don't think it fits here and the guidance should be changed. Consider this though, don't just agree with me, what do you think?
Before I give a view, I'll read what the rule actually protects, starting with `lib/api/fetcher.ts` and the commits that shaped it.
Read the API fetcher, its git history, the proxy's refresh logic, and the generated client's cookie handling.

I disagree that the rule is there for a retro feel. It rests on three concrete mechanisms, and I found each one in the code. I do agree it is broader than those mechanisms justify, and this dialog is where that breadth costs something.

## What the rule protects

1. **Session refresh happens in `proxy.ts`, and `proxy.ts` never sees `/api`.** An access token lasts 15 minutes (`../api/docs/authentication.md`). `proxy.ts` refreshes it before any page request or server action, but its matcher (`'/((?!_next|api|-/|auth/|.*\\.).*)'`) excludes `/api`. A member who leaves the profile open for 20 minutes and then uploads from the browser would get `401` with nothing to refresh the token. A server action is posted to the page URL, so it passes through `proxy.ts` and is refreshed first. This is the rule's strongest reason, and the rule's text never mentions it.
2. **`apiFetch` controls which headers and cookies reach the API.** It adds `X-Requested-With: sundial`, forwards only the six API cookies (commit `815acf1`: the join-draft cookie made Tomcat log invalid-cookie errors), and copies `cf-connecting-ip` so per-address limits apply to the member rather than the frontend server.
3. **`apiFetch` passes the API's `Set-Cookie` on to the browser** through `cookies()`, and `cookies()` exists only on the server. This is the part the rule's text does name.

## Where the rule is too broad

"A client component that needs data calls a server action" goes further than these mechanisms require. A browser request through the `/api` rewrite already gets same-origin cookies, and a `Set-Cookie` in the response goes straight to the browser. `next.config.ts` already sets `Cache-Control: private, no-store` on `/api/:path*`, and the Docker entrypoint injects the rewrite in production, so browser use of `/api` was planned for. Only the refresh has no answer yet.

For this dialog, server actions have real weaknesses beyond the missing progress bar:

- **A server action cannot be cancelled.** If the member closes the dialog during the upload, the upload still finishes on the server. The response goes back to a component that no longer exists, so we never learn the image id and cannot delete the image. It stays in storage until the 24-hour reaper removes it, and it has used one of the member's 30 uploads. With `fetch` and an `AbortController`, closing the dialog stops the request.
- **Polling through server actions queues them one behind another.** Next runs a page's actions one at a time, so 22 polls take up the page's only action queue for 30 seconds.
- **Uploads would need a larger request limit on every action.** `bodySizeLimit` applies to all server actions, not just the upload.

## Recommendation

Narrow the rule rather than delete it:

- **Server actions remain the default** for forms and for any write whose effect has to appear on a server-rendered page. `useActionState`, `useRestoredForm` and `revalidatePath` all assume that path. Attaching and removing the photo stay server actions for this reason.
- **A client component may call `/api` directly when it needs progress, cancellation or polling.** It does so through one small browser client, `lib/api/browser.ts`. That client sets the CSRF header, and on a `401` it calls `POST /api/auth/refresh` once and retries. It reuses the generated types, so no response shape is written by hand. In this feature, upload, poll and delete go through it.
- **`CLAUDE.md` is updated** to state the three mechanisms and this boundary, so the next reader understands why the rule exists rather than seeing a bare prohibition.

Two points need checking during planning, not assuming. The first is that Next's rewrite forwards `cf-connecting-ip` to the API unchanged. The second is whether orval can generate a second, browser-side output for the Images tag only, so that `lib/api/browser.ts` does not have to wrap each call by hand.

Do you agree with narrowing the rule this way rather than removing it?
Yes I think that's right. ../../prentora/frontend has a lot more client API calls and some kind of hook to refresh the tokens when needed on a 401. Should we have that here? Can we do?
I'll look at how prentora does it before comparing.
Looked at how the prentora frontend refreshes an expired access token on a 401 — its axios instance, and the refresh endpoint's actual behaviour.

Yes to both, and it is simpler here than in prentora because of how the Sundial API handles refresh.

## What prentora does

`lib/api/axios-instance.ts` is the single HTTP client for both server and browser, and orval generates React Query hooks on top of it. A response interceptor catches a `401` from anything outside `/api/auth` and `/api/public`, then calls `POST /api/auth/refresh`. If other requests fail while that refresh is running, they wait for it rather than starting their own (`isRefreshing` and `refreshPromise`). Each original request is retried once. If the refresh itself fails, the original `401` passes through to React Query's error handling.

## Why it is safe to copy here

Two facts about the Sundial API make it straightforward:

- **Refresh does not rotate the refresh token.** The endpoint description in `openapi.json` says it "issues a new access cookie", and `authentication.md` says the API "keeps no session table". A browser refresh and a `proxy.ts` refresh can therefore overlap without either invalidating the other. With a rotating token, whichever refresh finished second would sign the member out.
- **A rejected refresh already signs the member out.** It clears both cookies, and the endpoint description says "the caller can treat a 401 here as a completed sign-out." A failed refresh in the browser therefore means sending the member to `/login` with a `next` back to the current page. It does not mean showing an error.

## What I would build, and what I would leave out

`lib/api/browser.ts` is a `fetch` mutator with prentora's single-flight refresh:

- It sets `X-Requested-With: sundial`.
- On a `401` from any path outside `/api/auth/`, it waits for one shared refresh and retries the request once.
- A second `401`, or a refresh that fails, sends the member to sign in.
- It accepts an `AbortSignal`, so closing the dialog cancels the request.

orval generates a second output from `openapi.json`, filtered to the Images tag, with `lib/api/browser.ts` as its mutator. Browser calls then get generated, typed functions in the same way server calls do. Other tags can be added to the filter when a later feature needs them, and the server output stays exactly as it is.

I would **not** bring in React Query or axios. Prentora is built around client-side data fetching. Sundial renders on the server by design: the day side must be indexable, and the night side's rules live in routing and metadata, not in client logic. One dialog that polls does not justify a second data layer, and the polling loop is about 20 lines. If later features such as mail or notifications need client-side caching and refetching, React Query becomes worth reconsidering then.

## Next question

This decides one detail of the client. `fetch` cannot report upload progress in the browser, while `XMLHttpRequest` can. At our file sizes, a resized upload of 300 KB to 1 MB takes under a second on broadband and a few seconds on a weak mobile signal.

1. **Show "Uploading" with no percentage, and use `fetch` throughout (my recommendation).** One transport, and the upload stage usually disappears before a percentage would mean anything.
2. **Show a progress bar during the upload.** The upload call uses `XMLHttpRequest` inside the mutator, and every other call uses `fetch`.
Progress bar for this, I'd expect a common case to be a large image of several megabytes over a mobile network... though I suppose the resize in the browser means the upload is small?

Yes, the resize is what keeps the upload small. The several-megabyte original never leaves the phone.

A 12-megapixel phone photograph (4000×3000) comes out of the resize at 1280×960, which is 1.2 megapixels. As a JPEG at quality 0.92 that is usually 250 to 500 KB, and a very detailed scene might reach about 700 KB. These sizes are my estimate from typical JPEG compression ratios; I have not measured them. Upload speed on a good 4G connection is several megabits per second, so the upload takes under a second. On a weak signal of 0.5 Mbps, 400 KB takes about 6 seconds, and a busy indicator with no figure looks stuck by then. I think your instinct is right for that case. A progress bar costs one `XMLHttpRequest` branch inside the mutator, so I will include it. On a phone the resize itself can take a second or so, and the dialog shows "Preparing" during it with no figure, because pica does not report progress for a single image.

The questions are answered, so here is the design. I will present it in sections, starting with the pieces and where each one lives.

## Section 1: the units

### API (`../api`)

- **`PUT` and `DELETE /api/member/me/day-profile/image`, and the same pair under `night-profile/image`.** `PUT` takes `{ imageId }` and attaches the image, deleting the one it replaces. `DELETE` detaches and deletes the current image. Both lock the member row. The night pair also checks verification and an open night side. `PUT` completes the profile-photo checklist award, and it answers `409 IMAGE_SIDE_MISMATCH` or `409 IMAGE_NOT_ATTACHABLE` when the image cannot be attached.
- **`imageId` is removed from `DayProfileRequest` and `NightProfileRequest`.** The full profile writes keep whatever image is stored, and any code left dead by the change is deleted.
- **The description on `POST /api/member/images` gives the new schedule:** first poll at 400 ms, every 500 ms until 5 seconds, every 2 seconds until 30 seconds, then stop. It explains the figure by the three steps it has to cover.

### Frontend

1. **`lib/images/reduce-for-upload.ts`.** `reduceForUpload(file)` returns a JPEG `Blob`, or a typed failure when the browser cannot decode the file. It decodes with EXIF orientation applied, never enlarges the image, flattens it onto white, and uses pica in a worker to reach 1280 pixels on the long edge. ## What the server does to an upload

- **It accepts JPEG, PNG and WebP.** It refuses anything over 50 megapixels, and anything whose short edge is under 80 pixels after reduction.
- **It applies EXIF orientation, but only for a JPEG.**
- **It resizes only when the long edge is over 1280.** It uses Thumbnailator, then encodes the stored image as WebP at quality 0.82. If we send 1280 or smaller, the server does no resizing and only re-encodes, so our resize is the one the member sees.
- **It keeps transparency in the stored WebP** and flattens onto white only for the classifier and the hash.
- **It copies the raw EXIF segment out of the uploaded bytes** (`exifBase64`), JPEG only, and writes it to `image_hash_match` if the image matches a hash list. `../scratchpad/project-scoping.md` records that this field "holds the EXIF data Schedule 1 asks for, and nothing else keeps it". Schedule 1 is the list of items a National Crime Agency report must include.

## The problem

Drawing onto a canvas throws away all EXIF data. If the browser resizes every upload, `exifBase64` is always empty. A hash match would then produce a National Crime Agency report with no EXIF data, even though the member's original file carried it. The API docs already assume the frontend reduces images (`bunny.md`, "Decoding an upload"), but nobody connected that assumption to Schedule 1. The resize cannot ship without solving this.

## WebP or JPEG

**Send JPEG.** There are three reasons:

- The server re-encodes to WebP at 0.82 whatever we send, so a WebP upload does not improve the stored image.
- Safari's canvas cannot encode WebP. `toBlob('image/webp')` silently produces a PNG there.
- The server looks for EXIF only in a JPEG.

A high-quality JPEG (0.92) followed by the server's single WebP encode loses very little.

## Orientation

Orientation has to be applied exactly once. The canvas output carries no EXIF, so the server will not rotate it. The browser must therefore apply orientation while decoding (`imageOrientation: 'from-image'`). If the original EXIF were put back inside the JPEG we upload, its orientation tag would make the server rotate the photo a second time. That is why I do not recommend splicing the EXIF back into the file.

## Other points for the resize

- **The 80-pixel minimum** is checked in the browser, so the member sees the message before anything is uploaded.
- **Very large originals.** A 50-megapixel decode needs about 200 MB, which can crash a phone's tab. Above a browser-side limit of about 50 megapixels, matching the server's, the member gets the same message the server would give.
- **Transparency** is lost in a JPEG, so a transparent PNG is flattened onto white. This matches what the classifier sees, and a transparent profile photo is rare.
- **Wide-gamut photographs** from recent iPhones are converted to standard colour by the canvas and look slightly less saturated. Java's image library does not handle colour profiles well either, so the server does not preserve them today.
- **Classifier calibration.** `aws-rekognition.md` records that re-encoding an image moved one test photo across the day/night boundary. ## What a JPEG's metadata contains

A phone JPEG carries metadata in several places:

| Metadata | Where it lives | Still true after the resize? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EXIF (camera, time, GPS, orientation, maker notes) | `APP1` segment starting `Exif\0\0` | Yes, except orientation, dimensions and the embedded thumbnail |
| XMP (editing history, Apple and Google extensions) | Further `APP1` segments, sometimes several | Mostly |
| Colour profile (ICC) | `APP2`, sometimes split across several | **No.** The canvas has already converted the pixels to standard colour, so a Display P3 profile would mislabel them |
| Multi-Picture Format (iPhone gain maps, depth maps) | `APP2`, holding byte offsets into the file | **No.** The offsets point at data that is no longer there |
| IPTC and Photoshop data | `APP13` | Yes |
| Motion photo video, Samsung trailers | Bytes after the image's end marker | **No.** These can be several megabytes of video |

Copying every segment would therefore produce a file whose metadata contradicts its own pixels, and in some cases would upload a video we never intended to send.

What we *can* copy exactly is the `APP1` EXIF segment. EXIF's internal offsets are relative to its own header, so the segment stays self-consistent when moved. This segment is also all the server keeps: `ImageReducer.exifBase64` takes the first `APP1` with the `Exif` header and nothing else.

## Why splicing is still the riskier route

The EXIF segment includes the orientation tag. If we splice it back unchanged, the server rotates pixels the browser has already rotated. The only way to splice the segment untouched is to undo the browser's rotation before encoding, putting the pixels back as the sensor stored them. That means parsing the orientation ourselves and inverting eight different transforms. A mistake produces photos that are upside down or mirrored, and the result would depend on each browser applying orientation the way we assumed. A separate `exif` part sends the same bytes with none of that coupling.

So we stay with option 1. The browser extracts the EXIF segment from the original JPEG and sends it untouched as the `exif` part. The server verifies it starts with `Exif\0\0` and fits in one segment (65,533 bytes), and ignores it if not. It is used only as `exifBase64` and never for orientation.

## JPEG at 0.92, then WebP at 0.82

The two encodes do lose more than one would, but by very little, for these reasons:

- **Colour detail.** A browser JPEG stores colour at half resolution in each direction. Lossy WebP always stores colour at half resolution, so the stored image loses that detail whatever we upload.
- **Block artefacts.** JPEG compresses in 8×8 blocks and WebP in 4×4 blocks inside 16×16 macroblocks. Because the grids differ, WebP compresses JPEG's faint block edges as if they were detail in the photograph. At 0.92 those edges are faint, below what WebP at 0.82 keeps, so most of them are smoothed away instead of being preserved.
- **The final encode sets the quality.** The member sees the server's WebP at 0.82. If the stored photos ever look too soft, raising the server's `FULL_QUALITY` makes a far bigger difference than anything we upload.

The lossless alternatives cost more than they save. A 1280-pixel PNG is 2 to 3 MB, which brings back the slow mobile upload, and Safari cannot encode lossless WebP. I recommend 0.92. ## Why an integer fraction is better

My version decoded straight to 2560 pixels. For a 4000-pixel original that is a 1.5625:1 reduction, which is exactly the kind of uneven ratio where a browser's resampler aliases. Dividing the original by a power of two (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) avoids that, for two reasons:

- **A JPEG decoder can reduce by 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 while decoding.** libjpeg-turbo discards high-frequency detail during the decode itself, which is a proper low-pass filter, so no aliasing is introduced. I do not know whether each browser uses this route for `createImageBitmap`.
- **Browser resamplers are built around powers of two.** Chrome and Firefox build halved copies of an image (mipmaps), so a power-of-two reduction lands exactly on a level they filter well. A factor of 3 would not.

## Why Lanczos is still needed

The power-of-two step almost never lands on 1280. An 8000-pixel original divided by 4 is 2000, and 2000 down to 1280 is 1.5625:1 again. The fraction handles the large, even part of the reduction cleanly, and pica's Lanczos then handles the remaining uneven step, which is always between 1:1 and 2:1. That is the range where Lanczos gives its best results.

## The rule

Divide by the largest power of two that keeps the long edge at 1280 or more. Round the result to whole pixels. The rounding is off by under a pixel and has no visible effect.

## Two limits on the idea

1. **It may not save memory.** A browser is free to decode the full image and scale it afterwards, which would keep all the memory cost and add a resampling step I cannot inspect. I also still do not know whether Safari honours the resize options.
2. **It carries some quality risk,** because we cannot see which filter each browser uses.

I therefore recommend using the reduced decode only above 50 megapixels, where memory is the real risk. Everything below that, which includes a 48-megapixel iPhone photograph, is decoded in full and resized by pica alone, the path we can be most confident of.

The image upload dialog is built, reviewed and squashed into three commits, one per repository, all on `master`, none pushed:

- **frontend** `2b9f2f3` — the dialog itself: the browser client with session refresh, the pica-based photo preparation, the polling loop, the staged dialog and drop zone, and the profile page wiring with removal, on both sides.

Two things outside this plan's scope, found along the way and not fixed here:
- `npm run build` fails on `master` from before this plan started — `components/profile/edit/NightBodyPanel.tsx` pulls the server-only API client into a client bundle via `lib/member/night.ts`. Confirmed pre-existing (commit `4e31817`).
- A hard navigation to `/profile` throws during server rendering (`components/rewards/ReferralInvite.tsx:15` reads `window.location.origin` in a client component's render body). Also unrelated and pre-existing.

Task 10's real-photograph verification is in `$SCRATCH/verification/image-upload/` (not committed, per the plan — it's yours to check). `report.md` found no mismatches against the spec across nine photographs, including the over-100MP and 48–50MP fractional-decode cases, orientation, CMYK, transparency and the untouched-upload path. The one local-only finding, `upload_ip` staying `127.0.0.1` instead of the test header's address, is the deploy-time gap the brief itself anticipated (Tomcat's `remote-ip-header` is set only in `application-prod.yml`) — a real pre-launch checklist item, not a bug.
